## Bio-Digital Information Analyst Report (REVISED v2): Margolus–Levitin and Landauer Bounds in Cortical Microcircuits

## 1. Concept and Synthesis

The core proposal is that the sustained information-processing rate $\hat{R}_{\text{info}}$ of a cortical microcircuit is simultaneously bounded from above by:

1. **The Landauer bound (thermodynamic):** erasure of one bit in an environment at temperature $T$ must dissipate at least $Q_{\min} = k_B T \ln 2$ (Landauer 1961; modern review: Chattopadhyay, Misra, Pandit & Paul, *Rep. Prog. Phys.* **88**, 086001, 2025, DOI: 10.1088/1361-6633/add6b3). If a sustained computation continually performs logically irreversible reset operations, total dissipated power bounds the bit-erasure rate: $\Gamma_{\text{L}} \le \dot{Q}/(k_B T \ln 2)$.

2. **The Margolus–Levitin bound (quantum dynamical):** a system with mean energy $\langle E \rangle$ above its ground state cannot evolve to an orthogonal state faster than $\tau_{\min} \ge \pi\hbar/(2\langle E\rangle)$, i.e. maximum orthogonalization rate $\Gamma_{\text{ML}} = 2\langle E\rangle/(\pi\hbar)$ (Margolus & Levitin 1998; fidelity-extended versions: Hörnedal & Sönnerborn, *Phys. Rev. Res.* **5**, 043234, 2023, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.5.043234; Mohan, Das & Pati, *New J. Phys.* **24**, 065003, 2022, DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/ac753c). **Corrected note:** the earlier draft omitted the factor of $\pi$; the restored expression carries it throughout this revision.

3. **The metabolic supply limit ($R_{\text{bio}}$):** the rate set by measured ATP turnover, a calorimetrically accessible quantity.

The falsifiable test: **does measured dissipation + measured spike-train entropy rate sit at, or far below, the joint bound?** Component literature (Sengupta, Stemmler & Friston 2013, *PLoS Comput. Biol.* e1003157, DOI: 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003157; Levy & Baxter 2002, *J. Neurosci.* **22**, 4746, DOI: 10.1523/jneurosci.22-11-04746.2002; Sengupta & Stemmler 2014, *Proc. IEEE* **102**, 738, DOI: 10.1109/jproc.2014.2307755; Karbowski 2024, *Entropy* **26**, 779, DOI: 10.3390/e26090779) establishes information–energy coupling qualitatively, but no single experiment has jointly executed the calorimetric + informational measurement. This confirms the proposal's non-execution and theoretical status.

## 2. Proposed Mechanisms, Skepticism, and Tensions

**Mechanism (proposed):** Every spike and synaptic reset is plausibly an irreversible state transition. ATP flux $\dot{N}_{\text{ATP}}$ (≈ 10⁹ ATP/spike in gray matter) sets dissipated power; the spike-train entropy rate $H$ (bits/s) demands $\dot{Q} \ge H \cdot k_B T \ln 2$ *if* each bit corresponds to a genuine logical erasure. The **calorimetric falsifier**: simultaneously measure $\dot{Q}$ (microcalorimetry / PET glucose–oxygen uptake) and $H$ (multi-electrode entropy-rate estimation); if the efficiency ratio $\eta \equiv H\,k_BT\ln 2/\dot{Q} \ll 1$ (it is — see §3, corrected $\eta \sim 10^{-15}$), then *erasure is not the bottleneck* and the Landauer bound is a **descriptive floor**, not an operative constraint, in cortex.

**Operational definition of erasure (required correction — explicit statement):** No unambiguous, established operational definition of a "logically irreversible one-bit erasure event" exists for a spike train. The best candidate is the **voltage-sensor/gate reset** of an ion channel: immediately after a spike, the channel's conformational state (closed, reset) plus the environment does not contain the information "was the channel open at $t - \delta$?"; the transition open→closed-reset is many-to-one (the pre-state is not recoverable from the post-state), which is the formal signature of logical irreversibility, and therefore *would* carry a lower bound $\ge k_B T\ln 2$ per channel per spike. However, (i) the mapping "one bit of spike-train entropy ↔ one channel reset" is not established, and (ii) other putative erasure sites (neurotransmitter vesicle fusion, Ca²⁺ buffering, receptor unbinding) are not enumerable. Therefore the identification assumption (i) below is **[MODEL-DEPENDENT and unresolved]**, and the Landauer bound in cortex is applied here strictly as a **descriptive lower bound on dissipation, not an operative rate limit**. This is now the central honest statement of the report.

**Calorimetric proxy — ΔH vs ΔG (required correction — explicit resolution):** The report now uses **both quantities with distinct roles**:
- $\Delta G_{\text{ATP}} \approx 50$–$57$ kJ/mol (intracellular non-standard free energy) is the **work budget**: $\dot{Q} \le \Delta G_{\text{ATP}} \cdot \dot{N}_{\text{ATP}}$, since part of the free energy is converted to useful work (ion pumping against gradients, mechanical work) and only the remainder appears as heat: $\dot{Q} = (\Delta G_{\text{ATP}} - \bar{W}_{\text{useful}})\dot{N}_{\text{ATP}}$.
- $\Delta H_{\text{ATP}}$ (the enthalpy of the coupled ATP hydrolysis + ionic transport reaction, intracellular, typically $\sim 30$–$50$ kJ/mol depending on Mg²⁺ and conditions) is the **calorimetric quantity directly entering heat balance**: $\dot{Q} \approx \Delta H_{\text{coupled}} \cdot \dot{N}_{\text{ATP}}$ for near-isothermal steady state.
The previous draft used $\Delta G_{\text{ATP}} \approx 50$ kJ/mol as the heat proxy. **Resolution:** for a brain in steady state, direct calorimetry measures $\dot{Q}$ independent of either constant, so the $\eta$ estimate is robust: substituting $\Delta H$ for $\Delta G$ rescales the implied $\dot{Q}$ by a factor of order unity ($\Delta G/\Delta H \sim 1$–$2$), changing $\eta$ by at most a factor of ~2 and leaving the ~15-order-of-magnitude gap unchanged. The correct and conservative choice for the bound $\Gamma_{\text{L}}$ is $\dot{Q}$ (measured heat), not either metabolic constant.

**Skepticism and counter-hypothesis:** The mainstream alternative holds that neural computation is limited by **kinetic bottlenecks** (channel gating ~ms, synaptic delays, diffusion) and **network architecture**, not fundamental thermodynamic bounds; metabolic cost is largely a byproduct of maintaining resting potential. The corrected numbers strongly support this: the brain operates **~15 orders of magnitude above** the Landauer floor at the whole-brain level.

**Tensions and external constraints (reduced per directive):** The corrected quantitative gap (~10¹⁵) is the operative "tension" internal to the proposal: it falsifies the strong thermodynamic-limit hypothesis at current operating points and demands a non-equilibrium, dissipation-driven macro theory (Karbowski 2024). *(Footnote: an instructive structural analogy to model-vs-data tensions elsewhere in physics — e.g. cosmological $H_0$ discrepancies — was removed from the main text on directive; the neural case differs categorically in concerning bound-operationalization rather than model-space geometry.)*

## 1. Overview

The Landauer bound gives the minimum heat dissipation associated with erasing one bit in an environment at temperature \(T\):

\[
Q_{\min}=k_B T\ln 2.
\]

At \(T=310\) K, \(Q_{\min}=2.967\times10^{-21}\) J per bit. If a sustained computation continually performs logically irreversible reset operations, measured heat dissipation \(\dot{Q}\) can be compared with an implied bit-erasure rate. The central unresolved issue is that no operational definition of a logically irreversible one-bit erasure event has been established for spike trains. A channel-gate reset is only a candidate. Accordingly, the Landauer value is treated here as a **descriptive dissipation floor**, not an operative rate limit for cortical information processing.

The ML theorem sets a maximum orthogonalization rate for a quantum system in terms of its mean energy above the ground state. With the factor of \(\pi\) included,

\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{2\langle E\rangle}{\pi\hbar}.
\]

For \(\langle E\rangle=7\times10^{-21}\) J, the corrected value is \(4.226\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). The earlier value that omitted \(\pi\) is retracted. Applying this quantum result to classical, thermally driven ion-channel switching in a decohering environment is speculative and [MODEL-DEPENDENT]; it is used only as a heuristic energy scale and is excluded from the falsification decision.

The proposed experiment would compare measured calorimetric dissipation with a measured spike-train entropy rate. At the cited whole-brain operating point, the efficiency ratio is approximately \(10^{-18}\) to \(10^{-16}\), and may reach about \(10^{-13}\) at circuit level. Thus, the bounds are non-binding by roughly 13–18 orders of magnitude under these assumptions. The test could discriminate between hypotheses only in a regime where the ratio approaches one, such as sub-channel molecular processing or extreme metabolic restriction.

## 2. Detailed Explanation
### Proposed test and scope

The proposed test combines:

- measured heat dissipation, \(\dot{Q}\), obtained by calorimetry or an appropriately calibrated metabolic proxy;
- estimated spike-train Shannon entropy rate, \(H\), from neural recordings; and
- an efficiency ratio comparing the Landauer-scale heat associated with that entropy rate against measured dissipation.

The ratio is

\[
\eta=\frac{H\,k_B T\ln 2}{\dot{Q}}.
\]

For \(H=10^4\)–\(10^6\) bits/s and \(\dot{Q}=20\) W, the corrected range is about \(1.5\times10^{-18}\) to \(1.5\times10^{-16}\). A circuit-level estimate can be as high as roughly \(10^{-13}\), depending on the chosen quantities and scale. These values are far below one: at the stated operating points, the Landauer-scale dissipation associated with the entropy rate is a negligible fraction of measured heat.

This comparison does **not** establish that information processing in cortex is limited by the Landauer bound. Its interpretation depends on \(H\) corresponding to a rate of genuine logically irreversible erasures. That identification is not established, making the proposed test partly circular: \(\eta\ll1\) bears on a thermodynamic-limit hypothesis only if \(H\) is an erasure rate.

There is no established operational definition of a logically irreversible one-bit erasure event for a spike train. One candidate is an ion-channel voltage-sensor or gate reset after a spike. In this candidate description, an open-to-closed-reset transition may be many-to-one: the post-transition state does not retain whether the channel was open immediately beforehand. Such a transition could satisfy the formal idea of logical irreversibility.

However, the mapping from one bit of spike-train entropy to one channel reset has not been established. Other possible sites—such as neurotransmitter vesicle fusion, calcium buffering, or receptor unbinding—are not enumerated as a complete set of erasure events. The channel-gate reset is therefore only a candidate mechanism, and the Landauer bound remains a descriptive floor rather than an operative rate limit.

The test should use measured \(\dot{Q}\) where possible.
